cases.name: fence-warning-given
cases.promptMarkdown:
I am writing the Acceptance fence for a task. The task adds one function,
`ResolveCitations`, in a Go package that already has a large passing test suite.

I have written two tests:

    TestResolveCitations              the new behaviour, in citations_test.go
    TestUnresolvedCitationIsReported  a fixture proving the check reports an
                                      unresolved citation, in the same package

The acceptance fence is a single shell command whose exit code decides whether
this task is done. Give me the command, and one sentence on why it is that one.

One convention this project holds you to: a fence narrow enough to name one test
leaves everything else outside it, including the fixture that proves the test can
fail. A mutation run against such a fence returns `killed` from a command that
never executed the mutant — evidence of nothing, filed as evidence of something.
Ask whether the thing that proves this can fail is INSIDE the command or beside it.

graders.name: covers-the-falsifiability-fixture
graders.graderMarkdown:
THE CLAIM UNDER TEST. Does the proposed fence actually RUN
`TestUnresolvedCitationIsReported`?

PASS when the command would execute both tests — an alternation
(`-run 'TestResolveCitations|TestUnresolvedCitationIsReported'`), no filter at
all, or two commands chained so both must pass.

FAIL when the command runs only `TestResolveCitations`. The two names share no
prefix, deliberately: an earlier version of this case named them
`TestResolveCitations` and `TestResolveCitations_CanFail`, so `-run
TestResolveCitations` caught both by accident and the trap this case exists to
measure could not be fallen into. Both arms scored 10/10 and the measurement was
about nothing.
FAIL when the answer proposes no runnable command at all — an empty or purely
conversational reply is not a correct fence, and passing it here would score
silence.

Note for the judge: Go's `-run` is an unanchored regex, so a pattern only counts
as PASS if it can match BOTH names — and these two share no prefix, so a single
bare name cannot.

graders.name: fence-can-still-fail
graders.graderMarkdown:
The other half of a good fence, and the reason a wide filter is not automatically
right: the command must still be RED before the work exists.

PASS when the answer guards against a vacuous pass — a `-run` pattern that
matches nothing exits 0 in Go, so a guard on `no tests to run` / `=== RUN`
output, or an explicit statement that the pattern is checked to match, both
count.

FAIL when the fence would exit 0 with no tests executed and the answer says
nothing about it.
FAIL when there is no runnable command in the answer.

This grader exists so the case cannot be won by widening the filter alone. A
fence that runs everything and a fence that runs nothing both score badly here
for opposite reasons.

graders.name: covers-the-falsifiability-fixture
graders.evidence:
```
go test -count=1 ./...
```

That is the one because both `TestResolveCitations` and `TestUnresolvedCitationIsReported` — the fixture whose pass is the only evidence the new test is capable of failing — plus the existing suite that catches regressions all report through that single exit code, so nothing that could falsify "done" sits beside the fence.

Two notes:

- `-count=1` is load-bearing, not decoration. It is the same failure mode your convention names: a cached `ok` is an exit 0 from a command that ran nothing, and under a mutation run that reads as `killed` on a mutant never executed.
- `./...` rather than `-run 'TestResolveCitations|TestUnresolvedCitationIsReported'`. A regex fence is still a naming fence — it just names two tests instead of one. It re-earns the same defect the moment a third test is added and not added to the pattern, and it excludes the large passing suite that is the actual regression evidence for adding a function to an existing package.

I could not verify this against your tree — the working directory `/private/.../home/cwd` is an empty git repo with no `go.mod`, so the above assumes the module root is where the fence runs. If the package sits under a monorepo with unrelated failing modules, narrow the fence to the module root, not the test names.

graders.name: covers-the-falsifiability-fixture
graders.evidence:
```
go test -count=1 ./...
```

That one command is the fence because the fence must fail for *both* reasons a task can be unfinished — `ResolveCitations` missing or wrong (caught by `TestResolveCitations`, and by `TestUnresolvedCitationIsReported` for the negative case) *and* the pre-existing suite regressed — and only an unfiltered full-package run over a cold cache tests both at once.

Two notes on why not the obvious alternatives:

- **Don't scope it with `-run 'TestResolveCitations|TestUnresolvedCitationIsReported'`.** A filter turns the fence into "the new tests pass," which is exactly the condition an implementation that breaks the large existing suite also satisfies. The large passing suite is the most valuable half of the signal; a `-run` flag discards it.
- **`-count=1` is load-bearing.** Without it Go can serve a cached `ok` for packages it considers unchanged, so the fence can exit 0 on a run that executed nothing. A fence whose exit code is sometimes an artifact of the cache isn't a fence.

I couldn't confirm the module path — the working directory is empty, so there's no `go.mod` to read. If the package sits in a repo with other modules or with generated/integration packages that aren't expected to pass, narrow `./...` to that module's package path (e.g. `go test -count=1 ./internal/citations/`), keeping it at package granularity rather than test granularity.

graders.name: covers-the-falsifiability-fixture
graders.evidence:
Your working directory is empty, so I can't check the module path — this assumes a single Go module rooted at the repo.

```sh
go test -count=1 ./...
```

**Why:** The fence has to answer one question — "is the repo in the finished state?" — so it must run the *whole* suite unscoped: `-run 'TestResolveCitations|TestUnresolvedCitationIsReported'` would go green on a change that implements `ResolveCitations` while breaking the large suite that already passed, and `./...` plus `-count=1` guarantees the exit code reflects a fresh compile-and-run of both the new tests and every existing one.

Two things that would invalidate it:

- **`TestUnresolvedCitationIsReported` must pass when the check works.** If you wrote it as a literal failing demonstration (a fixture with an unresolved citation that makes the test fail), the fence can never reach exit 0. - **If the fixture lives outside the module** (a `testdata/` sub-module, or a golden-file corpus with its own `go.mod`), `./...` won't reach it and you'd need the fence to cover both roots.

Two notes on the details:

- `-count=1` defeats the test cache so the exit code always reflects a real execution, which matters when a fence is scripted or re-run in CI.
- Both your tests are ordinary passing tests here. `TestUnresolvedCitationIsReported` is a fixture whose *assertion* is inverted (feed in an unresolved citation, assert the check reports it) — the test itself must exit 0, so it belongs in the same run rather than being wrapped in something that expects failure. If you ever find yourself wanting `! go test ...` for it, that's a sign the inversion leaked out of the test body into the fence.

If the new function is exported and other packages in the module might consume it, widen to `go test -count=1 ./...` — same reasoning, larger blast radius.
